profile.summary: OmniNA is a generative foundation model for nucleotide sequences from many species. It was pretrained on 91.7 million DNA and RNA sequences from the NCBI nucleotide database, each paired with its text annotation, so that it learns to write an annotation for a sequence. After fine-tuning, it answers questions about an input sequence in natural language, for example whether it is a promoter, or which species it comes from.

summary_quotes.text: Here, we present OmniNA, a foundation generative model designed for comprehensive nucleotide sequence learning. The model was pre-trained on 91.7 million nucleotide sequences and the corresponding annotations encompassing 1076.2 billion bases and 197 million words spanning a multitude of species.
These data encompass genomic DNA and RNA sequences derived across diverse species.
OmniNA can be fine-tuned to align multiple nucleotide learning tasks with natural language paradigms.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OmniNA uses the LLaMA architecture, an auto-regressive decoder-only transformer. Sequences and annotations share one byte pair encoding tokenizer, built with SentencePiece and trained on nucleotide sequences and wiki-103 text, with 32,001 tokens. Each pretraining example is a prompt with three parts: an instruction, a nucleotide sequence and its annotation, and the model is trained to generate the text. Inputs are capped at 601 tokens. Fine-tuning casts each downstream task as a question and answer: the training file adds a question column, and the model learns to generate the answer.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper and README describe three sizes. The README table gives OmniNA-66M (8 layers, 8 heads, 66 million parameters), OmniNA-330M (16 layers, 16 heads, 330 million) and OmniNA-1.7B (24 layers, 32 heads, 1.7 billion). Hugging Face holds XLS/OmniNA-66m, XLS/OmniNA-220m and XLS/OmniNA-1.7B. The XLS/OmniNA-220m configuration has 16 layers and 16 heads, the shape the README gives for OmniNA-330M, so the middle checkpoint appears to be the same model under two different size names. The model card read (1.7B) holds only a licence tag. A result should name the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision; this page read 66m at 2c5e876a, 220m at 64ea6ce7 and 1.7B at 73d208a3.

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned OmniNA on 17 tasks covering sequence detection (taxonomy classification through genomic element detection) and species classification, and report that OmniNA-1.7B surpasses or rivals the compared methods. They also apply it to the effect of mutations on DNA and RNA processing. The authors themselves warn that test sets may overlap the training data of the compared models, and that converting regression baselines to classification may bias the comparison.

quotes.text: We demonstrate OmniNA-1.7B surpasses or rivals state-of-the art methods in 17 nucleotide tasks, encompassing nucleotide sequences detection and species classification.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Sequences and text annotations from the NCBI Nucleotide (nt) database up to April 2023, DNA and RNA from many species. Sequences over 3000 bp were cut with a sliding window, those under 200 bp dropped, and those with two or more consecutive Ns removed, leaving 91,732,311 sequences (1,076,183,408,570 bases) and 197,089,040 annotation words.

diagram.title: OmniNA workflow
diagram.caption: Sequences from NCBI nt are paired with their annotations in a prompt and used to pretrain a LLaMA decoder. Fine-tuning casts downstream tasks as questions, and the model generates the answer as text.

quotes.text: Nucleotide sequences, sourced from the NCBI nt database, are amalgamated with their corresponding text annotations for model pre-training.
The max length of input sequence is set to 601 tokens.
Fine-tuning is executed across 17 tasks in a Question-Answer (QA) framework.

gaps: No source shows how to run inference with a released checkpoint, or what prompt text a fine-tuned model expects at inference time.
Supplementary Figures 1 and 2 (model sizes and network structure) and the supplementary tables were not read.
Whether the released weights are the pretrained models only or include fine-tuned task heads is not stated.
Hardware needs for inference are not stated; the paper gives only the training system (NVIDIA DGX A100, 8 GPUs of 80GB).

review.note: Written from the xilinshen/OmniNA README, LICENSE, pretrain.sh and finetune.sh at commit 413a5288, the Hugging Face listing, the OmniNA-1.7B model card and the config.json files for XLS/OmniNA-66m (2c5e876a), XLS/OmniNA-220m (64ea6ce7) and XLS/OmniNA-1.7B (73d208a3), and the bioRxiv full-text page of 10.1101/2024.01.14.575543v1, each fetched on 2026-11-26. No command was executed and no human review is claimed.

no_run_guide_reason: The README gives package installs and two training scripts, but no inference example. pretrain.sh starts from a local folder (llama-220m/) the repository does not provide, finetune.sh starts from a local pretraining checkpoint (./output/pretrain/checkpoint-10/), and the model card read holds only a licence tag. A run guide would need commands the sources do not give.
notes: Size naming conflict worth a human look: the README table and paper say OmniNA-330M, while Hugging Face and the README install list say XLS/OmniNA-220m; the 220m config matches the 330M row's layers and heads. The GENEB leaderboard lists 'OmniNA-220m' with params 220000000 and an 'OmniNA' row; neither count was checked against the model's sources. The bioRxiv preprint has no reuse licence, so it is hashed and not stored. The repository and Hugging Face cards do not link to each other; the README names the XLS checkpoints, which is the link used here.
